utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Wednesday, June 25th, 2008, and I greet our witness, the representatives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj, as well as everyone helping us. We are holding this hearing in Courtroom II because there is Mr. Martic's appeal in Courtroom I, which is why we were sent to this courtroom. Mr. Seselj's cross-examination will continue. Mr. Seselj, you have 28 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Witness VS-1060, we left off with the topic yesterday, and that was the statement by Slavko Aleksic given to my legal advisers. From that statement, you were able to see that Slavko Aleksic is a citizen of Sarajevo, and from the very first days he took part in the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Serb combatant, and so in that case what you said doesn't hold true, doesn't stand, that Seselj's men came to the Jewish cemetery. You agree that they were there already. They were Sarajevo citizens. Some of them joined the Serbian Radical Party later on, declared themselves as Serb Radicals, and the people used to refer to them perhaps as "Seselj's men" in the popular form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were either called "Seselj's men" or "Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, "Chetniks," of course. I never forget to mention that concept and term here, either. Now I'd like us to look at a few documents that the Prosecution gave me, because I wanted to convince the Trial Chamber, as I was able to convince you, of some matters. They are documents which testify to the fact that Slavko Aleksic was, indeed, a citizen of Sarajevo, that he was politically active over there, he took part in the political life of Sarajevo, and later on he was militarily very active. He was active as a military man. And so I have here a document which was provided by the Prosecution. It was supposed to be a Prosecution exhibit, but as they're not going to use any of their exhibits, I'm going to use it as a provisional Defence exhibit. It's under 65 ter document 00995, and I hope you have that on e-court. Mr. VS-1060, these are the minutes. Can we have it up on the screen? Yes. It is the minutes from the 13th meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party of Novo Sarajevo, held in the municipality building on the 28th of February. It's an extraordinary session. 28th of February, 1992, at 1700 hours. Now, why is this meeting important? It is important because the president up until then of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party was replaced. One of the initiators of this replacement was Slavko Aleksic. He was from the local board of Gornji Kovacici so would you take a look at the members of the Municipal Board and take a look at number 11 and you will find of Slavko Aleksic there, that name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So on the 28th of February, 1992, he was still an official of the Serbian Democratic Party; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any insight into that, nor do I know about that. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. But this document was disclosed to me by the Prosecution, so you don't need to doubt its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't doubt its authenticity. I have the document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, this document shows at the end of February, 1992, he still wasn't a member of the Serbian Radical Party; isn't that right? He became a member somewhat later on? Slavko Aleksic doesn't remember the exact date, to be quite frank, because when he joined up, it just says "1992," and doesn't have the exact date. But, anyway, that was somewhat later, and to the best of my recollections it was in the second half of 1992, but that's not important. So this, then, is the first document that the Prosecution provided me with, and, Judges, since it had these documents in its hands, it could have rationalised the indictment a little bit and not to hold me accountable to something they know is a losing battle from the start. Then we have another document. It is document -- a document once again disclosed by the Prosecution, and it is a document under 65 ter. The number is 1478. 1478 is the document number, so may we have that displayed on our screens, please, as well. And this is a document dated the 1st of July, 1992. The document is from the Ministry of Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, The Security Services Centre Sarajevo, The Novo Sarajevo Public Security Station; and after that we have a list of the members of the reserve force of the police who executed duties and assignments of policemen in the Public Security Station of Novo Sarajevo and who needed to be paid our their salaries for June 1992. And the amount there is 6.000 dinars. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We're now going to look for the name here, the name of Slavko Aleksic. Here he is on page 2. Turn to page 2, please, and his name comes under 137 corrected to number 133. Can we see that portion? It's in the second shorter column, the second from the right, "Slavko Aleksic," his signature that he received a salary for the month of June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then that's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then at the bottom there is the signature of Arsenije Skipina, the Novo Sarajevo command, and that means that Slavko Aleksic has still not joined up with the Chetniks in June because he was in the police force at that time. So the unit which was called the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment to begin with, he had to establish after the month of June 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know when it was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said "towards the end of May," but you weren't quite sure that it was, in fact, the end of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say with certainty whether it was the beginning of June or end of May, because I didn't have an insight into when this unit was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I understand you. Now, you must understand me too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask for clarification of your question to the witness, because you said, and this is how it is reflected in the transcript, that Slavko Aleksic has still not joined up with the Chetniks in June because he was in the police force at that time. Is that based on the premise that he could not be a member of both, so does it necessarily follow that he would not have joined the Chetniks while still being in the police force? Is that a given fact?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Someone's either in the police or they're in the army. They can't be in the police and the army at the same time, Judge. A police unit can be subordinated in wartime to the army, but if someone's a policeman, he can't be a soldier at the same time. So quite obviously in June, he was still a policeman, and we have him here on the payroll and we see that he signed as having received his salary. And this is a Prosecution document. Therefore, it was after June that he left the police force and, with a group of like-minded locals, he established the Novo Sarajevo Detachment, and that detachment later on became the Anti-Armour Company, I think it was, of the 3rd Battalion of the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position of the Prosecution is he was both at the same time a policeman and a member of the Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have no answer -- no response to those nonsensical, nebulous statements. I don't even want to comment. Let the Prosecution deal with that itself. How can someone be a soldier and a policeman at the same time? I really don't know. I'll leave it to them. It's up to the Prosecution to fathom that one out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'd like some clarification. In the Territorial Defence, there were policemen as well as military people, wasn't there? I would like to ask the witness whether he knows about it. In the Territorial Defence, were there both military people as well as policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're the witness, so could you please answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is certain that there was not this delineation, as the accused is saying, there wasn't this separation, because that's how they behaved in May and June. The Serbian Republic organised its army sometime in May, so what the accused is now saying most probably means that the paramilitary units were preparing themselves at that time. Now, I don't know whether the Prosecution mentions paramilitaries or whether they came under the army organisation of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, in these units which you define as being paramilitary units, there was recruitment of policemen as well as military people, or volunteers coming from others and taken from the different parties, and were all integrated later on in the military forces? I'm talking about the military forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see. It was difficult to know that. I didn't know that they were volunteers, that the volunteers were coming. I didn't know how they were organised. I didn't know how the Chetniks were being organised. But I have to say that mention was made of the Chetniks at the end of May. Now, who organised them and how they were established, we didn't know that, or at least I didn't know that, but I heard -- as I say, I heard that the Chetniks were due to arrive at the end of May. I can't tell you what date exactly. Now, whether Slavko Aleksic was there or whether somebody else organised them, or whether they came from outside, from somewhere else, I really don't know. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But at the end of May, you didn't see those Chetniks, but you just heard that they were coming; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. We've clarified some matters up already, but let's deal with this. You're an intellectual and you must have known about these things, and I'm sure you know that before the war, the armed forces of the SFRY were divided into the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what existed before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Now, apart from them, you had the police force, the police existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was organised by the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But the army and the Territorial Defence came under the authority of the Ministry of Defence, whereas the police force was under the Ministry of the Interior; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So if somebody was a policeman, they came under the Ministry of the Interior, and at the same time that person couldn't have been a member of the JNA or a member of the Territorial Defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to put you right on that score. I have to put you right there. They could be in the police and also organise a Chetnik organisation or Chetnik detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, outside his working day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, this person, as a policeman, would have to earn his salary, right, and he belonged to a police unit or, rather, the reserve police force which is engaged during a war. And here on the document, we see this is a list of the reserve police force, so the reserve police force was mobilised because of the war that was on. Is that obvious from this document? Can we have the first page back, please, because in the heading it says that this is a list of the members of the reserve police force. Isn't that right? Do you see that at the beginning of the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to say that I was not able to know that. I could not have known that, nor could I have had an insight into all that organisation and what the police did and what the army did, because the Army of the Serbian Republic hadn't been organised to that extent yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. This isn't essential from the aspects of your testimony. I said that you testified very properly and correctly. But for me, it is important that through these documents, we clear up certain matters in principle. And you say that he could have been a member of the police, and apart from that he could have worked to organise the Chetnik detachments; is that right, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That isn't impossible. Perhaps he did do that, but while he was a member of the police force, he could not have been a member of that detachment; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he could have organised it. He could have worked to organise the defence along those lines, the defence of the territory that had been taken control of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I agree with that. But the moment that he became a member of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment or, rather, the Anti-Armoured Company within the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, he could no longer be a member of the reserve force of the police; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's clear, he moved and became a member of the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So from the moment he became a Chetnik, he could no longer be a policeman; that's the crux of the matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted you to confirm. Now I have another document here and we're going to look at this document under 65 ter, once again. It is 01479. And since the Prosecution has supplied me with all these documents and didn't want to use them, then I'm going to make use of them. This is a document of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is the Public Security Station of Novo Sarajevo. And members of the Armed Forces of the Bosut Barracks. Do you know where the Bosut Barracks are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Quite right. Now, it says: "List of reserve police employees," of employees who worked in this police station in the course of July 1992 and who were given an advance salary payment for the month. And you can see that he was reassigned as a policeman to the Armed Forces of the Bosut Barracks, but he was still being paid in July by the police force. He still received his salary from the police force, and this is the last document of that type which I have at my disposal, and I don't think the Prosecution has any other documents either. And you can see that here that he is first on the list of five people, that he received a salary for July, and that it amounted to 11.000 dinars; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now we come to what we were missing earlier on; isn't that right? This is his transition, when he moved from the police to the armed forces, right, to the Bosut Barracks above the Jewish cemetery; right? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief -- at the beginning of the cross-examination, the witness said that Aleksic -- a couple of times, saw Aleksic during the war. He didn't know what he was doing before the war. He didn't know Aleksic before the war, so I don't know how the witness can comment on all these documents. If Aleksic was a member of the police, he was a member of the Chetnik movement, how he was paid, from who, and so on. I don't know these documents can be used in that way with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the written statement you made, on paragraph 11 you said that you saw Mr. Slavko Aleksic, but you gave no date. There is no date, actually. Now, this being said, we need to know whether you saw him in May, or June, or later on. The documents shown to us by Mr. Seselj seem, and I say "seem" to establish that this person was a reserve policeman, was reporting to the MUP, so as far as I know, either you're a soldier or a policeman. During a military operation, you may be resubordinated to the military command, but there needs to be some kind of document for this transfer. When you told us you saw him, this Aleksic, are you sure you saw him in May or June, or did you see him later on? You stayed there until November 1994. Of course, several years later it's very difficult to know exactly when it was. I, myself, would be totally unable to say that I saw someone in May years ago. I would be unable to do so, to say so. So how can you state that you saw him either in May or June, or did you rather -- would you rather say, "I did see him, I'm sure, but I can't really be sure about the date when I saw him"? What's your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know when I saw him, but I certainly didn't see him in 1992. I saw him later on. I know that Chetniks began to be mentioned in late May 1992. I didn't see Slavko Aleksic either in May or in June, nor did I know what his movements were with respect to the police and the Chetnik unit established either by Aleksic or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say what the year was, but when I saw him, I saw him with a subara hat on, so it was in wintertime. He wouldn't be able to wear such a uniform in summertime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... during the winter, because he had this fur hat, and it's not in the summer, when it's 30 or 35 degrees. But the document we have here dates from the month of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another problem, except, you know -- other than the problem of the date, which is also very relevant. This is my problem: We're talking about members of armed forces. You did your national service, and maybe you know. If you don't know, of course, tell us. But since you did your national service, tell us whether there were two different institutions, the armed forces and the army, in the former Yugoslavia. I believe - I'm not really sure, and we'll see that maybe through other witnesses, or maybe you can help us understand this - so the same law ruled the military situation in Republika Srpska, which meant that they were the armed forces, and during a state of war the police was part of these armed forces, and there was also the army, which is another institution. So the police and the armed forces -- and the army made up the armed forces. During a state of war, the police was part of the armed forces. Was that the way it was or am I wrong? If I'm wrong, of course tell me, but I would like to know also whether, in a state of war, these armed forces were all placed under the command of the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that I'm not aware of how the command was organised, but under the law there should be a single command. When the army was organised in the Republika Srpska, it should have had a single command. I served in the army, and I'm aware that that's the sort of organisation that should have been in place. So the Territorial Defence, the police and the armed forces all had to be under a single command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it clear that five members of the reserve force of the police for some reason were transferred to the armed forces, but the police continued paying their salaries for the month of June; is that clear to you from this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that his salary was paid to him afterwards, because the Chetnik unit was being organised separately and they didn't have any funds, perhaps, so it's possible he received his salary later on, afterwards, after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. We have another page within this document. Please turn to the second page. It's dated the 2nd of August, 1992. It's also issued by the Ministry of the Interior, the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo. So there's a list of members of the armed forces who are carrying out assignments at the Bosut Barracks and who received salaries for July 1992, in the approval of the chief of the Security Services Centre. So Arsenije Skipina, the commander, calls these five people, members of the armed forces, but he's paying their salary for July; is that clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- it's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There are 16 names here. 11 have been crossed out. Only five have been circled. Those are the five on the first list. So somebody probably asked for 11 men, and 11 were designated and some returned, but 5 remained within the armed forces, and that was in July. This confirms my point, doesn't it, that he moved from the police to the army? Do you agree that that would be the logical interpretation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that he could have worked on organising Chetnik units while receiving a salary from the police, because where else could he have received his salary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that a kind of question, "Do you agree it would be the logical interpretation," I don't think can be admitted. The witness can't answer on these documents because he's not a policeman, he's not a member of the Ministry of the Interior and so on. The witness doesn't know anything, as I say, about this matter, so I don't feel that we can continue the cross-examination on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will decide what probative value it will give to the answer. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I have to draw your attention to the following: The circumstances of the wartime events in Grbavica are included in the indictment, and alleged crimes are ascribed to me which were committed by Slavko Aleksic and his unit. This is the only witness planned by the Prosecution to prove this. You have already seen that there were no crimes, that there is no criminal responsibility of Slavko Aleksic and members of his unit. The OTP obtained these documents, but did not tender them today. There is no other witness through whom they can be tendered, because there is no other witness for the general area of Sarajevo, so they put these two documents on the 65 ter list without ever intending to use them. But to their -- unfortunately for them, I went through these documents and found those that were useful to me. What can I do when I'm so capable and the OTP so inept? Something has to be done to establish a balance. A kind of tutor or warden should be imposed on the prosecution to show them how to do their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't start again or we'll have to redact what you are saying. You cannot make these statements, broad statements on the competence of the Prosecutor and the Prosecution. You can't do that. Otherwise, we'll redact everything, or we're just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Judge, I would accept your position fully had you said the same when the OTP said they would again ask that counsel be imposed on me because I'm incapable of defending myself, and yet they pretend that they are capable. I'm constantly showing you how inept they are, and you can redact whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, so far the Trial Chamber has seen no motion as far as this problem of counsel is concerned, so the Trial Chamber has not even looked into this yet. Why are you accusing the Trial Chamber of different things? I really don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, proceed. I believe you have some time left, 10 to 15 minutes. What you said so far is on the transcript. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In light of what the accused has said, it might be appropriate for the Prosecution to clarify that the documents that the accused seemed to seek admitted through this witness, in our respectful submission, are not admissible through this witness, because the witness is not a witness who has knowledge of police matters. It's not a witness who has knowledge of military matters. And the accused seems to be presenting these documents as evidence in support of the Defence case, which he can do in due course. I refer Your Honours to Exhibit number P217, which is also relevant to this issue, and basically what the accused is doing is he's making submissions rather than just cross-examine the witness within the area of his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have 13 minutes left. I don't know whether you're going to ask for these documents to be tendered. Will you ask for these documents to be tendered, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, how can you expect me to tender Prosecution documents? I'm using them in my cross-examination. That's the tactics of my Defence, which fits into the overall strategy of my challenging all the counts of the indictment. For me to tender Prosecution exhibits, well, I'm not crazy enough to do that. Why should I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You've answered, so please continue. You have 13 more minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll have to cut short what I had planned to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The document I showed you yesterday marked Roman numeral II, it's a statement by Colonel Ratomir Maksimovic. We'll comment on some parts of this statement, because I'd like to know what you know about this. Colonel Maksimovic handed me this statement in Belgrade. It was authorised in the 4th Municipal Court. He's willing to be my Defence witness, but only if I call him as a Defence witness will he testify. So let's see what he says here. He says: "During the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was in the Department for Morale and Information in the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I arrived in the Command on the 1st of April, 1993, with a rank of colonel." Have you ever heard of Colonel Ratomir Maksimovic in the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had an opportunity to hear about the people who are on the territory of attack on Sarajevo or to meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says that on several occasions, he toured the units deployed in the defence of Grbavica. He says that this was the most dangerous position throughout the war, all of Grbavica was under the control of Muslim fire, the Muslim forces held a dominant positions of Mojmilo and Debelo Brdo and so on, and he goes on to explain the significance of the Jewish cemetery, and around the middle of the third paragraph, he says the following: "The fall of the Jewish cemetery and its linking up with Debelo Brdo which was under Muslim control would have had disastrous consequences for the entire Serbian population of Grbavica and the villages at the foot of Mount Trebevic. The unit," that's his unit, "controlled the line from the top of the Jewish cemetery to Debelo Brdo. Aleksic did not have responsibility over the urban parts of Grbavica. His line of defence implies the area in the countryside, where it was difficult to move around. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the threat to the population, well, had there been no war and the attack by the Serbian Army, certainly they would not have been in danger, so probably the Jewish cemetery was selected for strategic reasons and it was divided into parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1060, we belonged to different sides in this war, according to our intimate feelings, and we cannot agree. We cannot agree on who is to blame for the war either, can we? We cannot agree on these points, and there's no need for us to discuss them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that we shouldn't even discuss these things, but I do wish to mention that this was not a civil war. It was the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it's pointless to discuss whether it was not a civil war, and we shouldn't waste time on things that I had no opportunity of learning about or knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the fight was between those who wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to be independent and those who wanted it to remain within Yugoslavia. Is that the most general sort of definition on which we might agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be very difficult for the two of us to discuss this, I as a witness and you as an accused, because other things happened before Yugoslavia fell apart, and you are well aware of that. You are an intellectual and you know how things went in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, to cut this story short, do we agree that the Jewish cemetery, for the Serbian forces and for their aims, was the most significant point in the entire Grbavica area? Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do, because it was from that hill above the Jewish cemetery that they had more control over the central part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had the Muslims taken control of the Jewish cemetery, then all the areas of Trebevic and Lukavica would have fallen, all the slopes around there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say. I'm not a strategic expert, so I don't know what would have happened afterwards. That is just something that we can suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's see what Colonel Maksimovic says: "I met Aleksic when he came to the Corps Command on one occasion, and when we analysed things in the Corps Command, nothing negative was ever said about him. Quite the contrary. His unit held the defence line. They were very disciplined and in keeping with the concept of the Corps Command." Now, do you have any facts to present here which could challenge this assertion of Colonel Maksimovic here in this statement of his?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Maksimovic interprets this from his own angle. That's how he sees things, so I can't comment, nor do I have the right to speak about the matter, because I don't know what his intentions were. He is defending the Serbian Republic here and Aleksic, and he is even praising him, so I can't enter into things like that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Let's see what he says about the work obligation. He says: "Aleksic," and this is still on page 1, "never undertook anything on his own initiative or without the knowledge of the Corps Command. He acted exclusively pursuant to orders. The Army of Republika Srpska did not have anything to do with work obligations. That came under the authority of the civilian authorities, the municipalities which functioned normally, and the work obligation held true for all the fit adult population, without any discrimination. It applied to the Serbs and the Muslims and everybody else." So is that correct, what Colonel Maksimovic says there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's shameful that he should have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, all able-bodied Serbs. All able-bodied Serbs were engaged in the army, those who could put up a defence, and all those who were over the age of 65 were exempt. Up to age 65, they were in the army. So this is not substantiated here, and you shouldn't take this into account as a valid observation and interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But do you know that in 1992, for instance, the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Novo Sarajevo was functioning? Did you hear of the existence of this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't have known of the existence of the Crisis Staff, but I assume it could have existed, although I didn't take part in it. I was in the work platoon, digging trenches and making bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This Crisis Staff, as one of its tasks, had the food supply for the civilian population, and it was its task to supply the Grbavica population with food at a rate of 50 per cent of what was needed in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who made that observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that the population received humanitarian aid from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did UNPROFOR distribute humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, UNPROFOR always did that. It always followed the trucks, bringing in supplies, so I saw the soldiers from France and other countries that acted as escorts and followed these trucks. So this was supplies not from the Serbian Republic, but the Serbian Republic distributed what it received from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it wasn't the UNPROFOR soldiers that distributed the supplies, it was the state employees of the Serbian Republic; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that humanitarian aid did come in and that the UNPROFOR soldiers served as an escort, accompanying the supplies, and stored it in warehouses, and then of course there was an organisation that distributed the food to the citizens, the supplies to the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it is your assumption that all those food supplies distributed by the state organs of the Republika Srpska came from UNPROFOR; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we thought, that it was coming from UNPROFOR, that supplies from UNPROFOR were distributed, and that was mostly food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it wasn't the UNPROFOR soldiers that distributed the food to you, but the employees of the Serbian Republic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear from you. Now let's have another document on our screens under 65 ter again. D1401 is the number, 01041, and this is a report of the work of the Crisis Staff of the 5th of June, 1992. It is signed by the president, Radomir Neskovic, and he says -- he talks about food for the population in one section. Just move down one line, please. Thank you. It says the local communes made up lists of civilians with their first and last names, and it was according to these lists that food supplies amounting to 50 per cent of peacetime supplies were distributed to those on the lists. Is it true that the food you received and that you say was procured by UNPROFOR, is it true and correct that it amounted to about 50 per cent of peacetime supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that, I can't claim that that was so, because I wasn't included into any of that. All I do know is that I had to go and collect the supplies where they were stored, what each citizen had a right to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. But what you received during the month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have one more minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We won't dwell on food and food supplies. I'm going to use up my minute in this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned the case when you were digging trenches and making bunkers along the embankment of the Mijetska River, and you said that next to you, right beside you, Enes Hadziahmetovic was killed, and you assume he was killed by this man, Aleksandar Trivkovic. While you were building a wall, he went to a building. Two shots were fired, Enes was killed and the second bullet missed you. Is that a proper interpretation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that that was what the others present had concluded as well, because he just left us there, the two of us there. He went off. We continued working. We were standing up and working. And then quite suddenly two bullets were fired, and I know where they hit. I was not able to claim this for a fact, but that's the assumption, that that's what he did. But I have to add this: It's very strange that somebody claims that they don't know that the man -- that the soldier existed at all, whereas his neighbours, who were working and engaged in trench-digging, knew each other very well because they were neighbours. And he was born near the Drveni Most, the Wooden Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't have much time. It's not important. The people who I've contacted know nothing about this man. Anyway, you have no proof and evidence that he did the shooting. You didn't see him shoot, but you and the people around you assumed that it could have been him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the bullets could have been from a sniper fired from the Muslim side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we were in such a place that it couldn't have been the Muslim side, as you say, who fired the bullets, the sniper fire from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you able to establish where -- which direction the bullets had come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the opposite residential building opposite to the Zeljeznicar football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that the building that Trivkovic went in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trivkovic went there. Now, where the shooting came from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you have no proof and evidence that he did the shooting, that he targeted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him, but that is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's round that up. That's just your assumption and not something you know for a fact on the basis of proof and evidence, that he did the shooting. And I assume that is enough for the minute that I had left. If my minute isn't up, I'll be happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sometimes one minute becomes a stretched minute, it can be long. But does the Prosecutor have any redirect? Mr. Ferrara?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in the direct examination yesterday, you affirmed there were Seselj men in Grbavica amongst the various volunteers. As well as in your statement, where you mention the presence of Seselj volunteers in Grbavica five times. In paragraph 9, 11, and 15 the word volunteers is used five times in English version and at least three times in the B/C/S version. However, in the cross-examination you say, and I quote: "I never say and I never knew and I hear this for the first time now that there were volunteers, Seselj men or Chetniks. I --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I didn't finish my question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I stepped in with an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please wait for the Prosecutor to finish his question before you raise an objection. I don't even know what the Prosecutor wanted to say. Yes, please go on, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. However, in the cross-examination, you say, and I quote again, it's transcript 8628, lines 4 to 7: "I never said and I never knew, and I hear this for the first time now, that there were -- that there were volunteers, Seselj men or Chetniks. I never said that. I didn't know that they were volunteers." So my question is this: Please let us know what your final answer were, the one you gave in the examination-in-chief and the statement or the one you gave during the cross-examination? Were there volunteers in Sarajevo, and in Grbavica in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor cannot draw attention to the witness for contradictions among the things he said in his statements and during the testimony, because the witness testified here in the court, whereas the statement was written for him by the Prosecution, in the previous statement. So what it says in the previous statement is not the witness's responsibility, it's the Prosecution's responsibility, and how that came to be in the statement, we should examine the Prosecutor. So you can't have the Prosecutor trying to catch the witness out in contradictions of this nature. That is quite improper. The Prosecutor can only deal with what the witness stated here in court, and nothing other than that, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree with Mr. Seselj. Maybe there is a misunderstanding in the interpretation, because I say at the end of my question "in the direct examination the witness affirmed there were Seseljevci volunteers in Grbavica," as well as in his statement; not only in the statement, but also in the examination-in-chief. Later on in the cross-examination, he said exactly the opposite, so the contradiction is between what he said in the examination-in-chief and what he said in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not true, and I have to tell you something else. I asked the witness whether he had heard that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, or Seselj's volunteers, whichever you like, whether they came to Grbavica 2 and took part in the fighting for Hrasno, because a group was surrounded there, so I referred to the transcript from the intercepted conversation. And the witness said that he had heard nothing about that, and the witness confirmed several times that Slavko Aleksic's unit he considered to be Seselj's men and that he considered them to be Chetniks, and that that was one and the same as far as he was concerned. So whenever he says "Chetniks," and "Seselj's men," he's speaking exclusively about the unit of Slavko Aleksic. And as for the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party group which in April of 1992 fought in Grbavica 2, (redacted) (redacted), he'd never heard of this group on Grbavica 2. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One more reason to put to him this question, just to elucidate this contradiction. So, Mr. Witness, could you please answer the question that the Prosecutor asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The interpretation wasn't correct here. I said that Seselj's Chetniks existed, or Seselj's men, or "Chetniks," but I said that I'd never heard of them being volunteers. I did say that volunteers came, Russians, Belorussians and others, but not within the formation of the Chetniks. So that's not the same thing. And let me repeat once again, please: We knew where the Chetniks were and Seselj's men were, but I never heard of volunteers up until now, up until Mr. Seselj mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is what I understood yesterday. It was very clear. Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to make sure we understand you even better, so when we talk about Chetniks, those were soldiers of the Republika Srpska who were qualified as Chetniks; they were Chetniks, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let me repeat once again. The Chetniks or Seselj's men, "Seseljevci," as the people called them, they were one army. Now, whether they belonged in command terms, and I mentioned that several times, to the Serbian Republic, to the army or not, I don't know that. However, they did exist. Now, were they volunteers in the Chetniks? I don't know that. That's something I could not have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry, but I'm not sure I understood you correctly. According to this name that people were giving them or that you were giving to them, those were all the soldiers of the Republika Srpska who were called "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you didn't understand, I'll repeat it again. What was in existence was the Army of the Serbian Republic. Now, I don't know according to what command the command establishment was between the Chetniks and the Serbian Army, but the Chetniks, or Seselj's men, whichever you like to call them, were one army, and that army was stationed at the Jewish cemetery. They were one group of soldiers. Now, which command they belonged to and how they were established, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we should think of putting the question to the witness this way: Witness, could you explain to us, what is, according to you, the difference between "volunteers" and "Chetniks"? What is the difference between these two categories, to your mind? How do you make a difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that at all, and let me repeat again, I didn't know that the volunteers existed, except for the ones I mentioned from Russia, Belorussia and so on. I didn't know that volunteers existed. I don't know to this day whether they belonged -- well, to who these volunteers belonged to. Mr. Seselj mentioned the fact that the volunteers arrived from the Radical Party from Serbia, but I did not know that, nor could I ever have said that I knew about them, about cases like that, because I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: In the cross-examination, transcript 8646, line 19, you said that it would have been better had the Grbavica police station not existed at all. What did you mean by this? Can you clarify your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, you see. Here's why I said that: There was looting at Grbavica, and everybody acknowledges that, and Mr. Seselj acknowledges it too. And I believe him when he says that there could have been looting. At least that's what he says. But they did absolutely nothing to prevent the looting that was going on at Grbavica and the other parts taken over by the Serbian Republic. That's why I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who was in charge in this police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the Ministry of the Police of the Serbian Republic, that they disposed of that police station at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: In the cross-examination, using the statement by Aleksic and this military booklet, Mr. Seselj sought to show that despite Aleksic being a Chetnik leader, the volunteers, fighters he controlled, were not organised by this party. It's transcript 8642, lines 11 to 20. Madam Registrar, please, can we show to the witness the Exhibit P217. This is the Seselj order number 124, dated 13 May 1993, admitted as Exhibit P217, for the proclamation of Chetnik vojvoda, and it states that: "Slavko Aleksic, son of Ilija, Serbian Chetnik vojvoda, has been a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Serbian Radical Party since their establishment, participating activity and organising and promoting the idea of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Serbian Radical Party in Sarajevo and the surrounding area. When the Muslim paramilitary units began terrorizing the Serb population, he immediately organised, trained and personally led all the actions of the volunteer units of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?" As far as you know, when you saw Aleksic, was he surrounded by Chetnik volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim once again that I never mentioned volunteers, nor could I have known who was a volunteer and who wasn't. I could have just seen something in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When you saw Aleksic, was he surrounded by Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was surrounded by Chetniks or other soldiers, I couldn't know that. Or if they were Chetniks, then they had long beards, that's all I can say, and long hair. But you could have people looking like that and being other types of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor is now torturing the witness much more than he objected to the way in which I was cross-examining. How could the witness know this? This is a proclamation from 1993, and only in a few sentences, in concise form, do we have something about Aleksic's merits. And among those, it says that he joined the Serbian Chetnik Movement, the Serbian Radical Party, from its very inception. But from its inception in Sarajevo, not from its founding in Belgrade, because the party was founded in Serbia on the 23rd of February, 1991, whereas it was formed in Sarajevo only in 1992, and the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik Movement, both. And we saw when that would have been according to his membership in the Serbian Democratic Party. Now the Prosecutor is trying to make the witness say something that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara, the only important element with regard to the proclamation of Mr. Aleksic as a vojvoda is the sentence where it says he was named commander of the Chetnik detachment of Novo Sarajevo, that's all, so put a question to the witness only with regard to this, because for the rest it's a wastes of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you ever see Aleksic wearing a uniform of the VRS army with the insignia of his alleged rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Today, in page 19, 20, lines 23, 25, 13 of page 20, you answered to the following question of Mr. Seselj: "Well, do we agree that the Jewish cemetery for the Serbian forces and for their aims was the most significant point in the entire Grbavica area; do we agree on that?" And you answered: "Yes, we do, because it was from that hill above the Jewish cemetery that they had more control over the central part of Sarajevo." Can you explain, what did it mean to have more control over the central part of Sarajevo? Should it be easiest for snipering on the central part of Sarajevo from this point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I don't have further question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, on my behalf and on behalf of the Trial Chamber, we thank you very much for coming to The Hague to testify. I wish you a safe journey home. Before you leave this courtroom, we will make a 20-minute break, which will enable you to exit this courtroom slowly, and we'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when you grew up, how was the relationship between the different ethnicity in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to praise my village and the surrounding area. Never, until I reached the age of 22, did I notice that somebody was looking at me in a different way because I belonged to a different ethnic group or a different religion. We really lived well, in harmony. And I can also confirm that my village, Kostijerevo, is a mixed village. There are Serbs living there as well. It would be difficult to find another such place in Bosnia-Herzegovina where people lived in such harmony.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this relationship changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say that. In a way, it started when the national, or "nationalist," at some people called them, parties were established starting in 1990. At the rallies where these parties were promoted, one could observe national insignia, people wearing historical uniforms from World War II, and this indicated that the friendship and harmonious coexistence was starting to crumble.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you attend any of these rallies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never attended any political rally or the founding of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you describe any further facts showing how the relationship changed, not only referring to the political rally but in the daily life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relationships didn't change all that much when the parties were established, but they deteriorated suddenly when the conflict broke out in Croatia. The Serbs from Bosnia volunteered, let's say, to go to war in Croatia, or they might have been mobilised; I don't know. But I do know one thing. Some Bosniaks in my village received call-up notes, but they tore them up and threw them away. I asked a man of Serb ethnicity, whom I knew well - he was from Drinjaca - I said to him, "What does this mean if somebody gets rid of a call-up note saying he should report to a barracks in Tuzla?" And he just shrugged his shoulders and said, "Oh, forget about that." So nobody was mobilised or went to volunteer or to report, of their own free will, to those barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When you say that at these rallies one could observe national insignia or people wearing historical uniforms from World War II, do you know what kind of insignia or what kind of uniform they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did have an opportunity of seeing on television, what this looked like. The cameras took pictures. In the case of Serbs, I saw them wearing Chetnik uniforms, the sort that were worn in World War II, and also cockades. There were people in T-shirts with eagles, and there were unusual flags being brandished, and I saw all that on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did it come a time when the Serbs started organising autonomous guards in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war in Croatia, we had joint guards together with the Serbs. At that time, I was employed in Belgrade. One evening, I returned home and found my older brother with an M-48 rifle, but I knew he didn't have a rifle. So I asked him, "Where did you get this rifle?" And he said, "Well, we have joint guards with the Serbs in the village, under the pretext because the Serbs said that there should be guards in case somebody tried to infiltrate our area from the outside and sow dissent among the people." And I asked him who had organised this, and he gave me a name and he said, "We are now changing shifts. You can join in if you like." And I said I didn't want to because I would be staying only for a short time and I would have to go back to work again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did it come a time when this joint guards or mixed guards was stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these joint guards stopped when the war ended in Croatia. I think it was in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November, I finished my work in Belgrade and came home for my winter vacation. My employer, for whom I worked in a private company, sent someone to escort me to the bus. I asked him why, and he said, "Well, things are happening in Belgrade. All sorts of things are going on. I just want you to board the bus safely." And he told this man, who drove me to the bus stop, to see me off. I found this very odd, although I'd seen all sorts of things in Belgrade, nationalist incidents against Muslims, and I myself had been in a scrape like that, and I might even have lost my life, but I was saved by a man, a restaurant owner. When I arrived in Kostijerevo, I saw that there were no longer any joint guards, so I asked what was going on, "Why aren't there any guards anymore?" And at that time in 1992, there was to be a referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so I learned from my family that they no longer wanted to have joint guards together with us because we had already decided to vote in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina seceding from the rest of Yugoslavia. Some political parties were calling for something like that. So that was the end of cooperation with the Serbs in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So when you say that they no longer wanted to have joint guards, what do you mean? Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these Serbs from my village. They said, "How can you want us to continue keeping guard together when you're being called to referendum and we see that you're all going to vote in favour of secession, and we want to stay in Yugoslavia. We had a good time in Yugoslavia, we lived well." And we said, well, yes, we did, but Yugoslavia is no longer what it was, it's no longer what it used to be, and it's no longer entire, it's no longer intact, and one can no longer even call it Yugoslavia. And then they said, "Well, you see, Serbia, Montenegro and Bosnia, well that's enough for a good, strong Yugoslavia to continue to exist."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: At that point, you [indiscernible] them. Did you organise the guarding of your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that point on, separate guards were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you participate in this guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did, yes. Every evening, we went out. The guards were held only at night in the village, simply to make sure that nobody passed through the village and saw us all asleep and threw a hand grenade or caused an incident, something that might then cause a conflict or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of uniform or weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any kind of uniform. But as for weapons, we had hunting rifles which we borrowed from neighbours who had them, and then we passed them on to the next shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many rifles did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six, six hunting rifles. One was a traditional and one carbine which looked like an M-48. There were hunters in the village who had licenses for those weapons, and they lent them to us, so we all kept guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When was your village attacked, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village was attacked on the 30th of May, 1992. I remember well. We had spent the whole night before that in the woods. What I want to say is for a month before that, we often slept in the woods. We abandoned our houses at night and then went back to them in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Before the date of the 30th May 1992, did someone come to your village on 19 [sic] April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Sorry, 29, I'm sorry, 29, not 19.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th, you mean, April?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of April, 1992, the Yugoslav People's Army, with its reserve force, mobilised men of the -- of Serb ethnicity who had uniforms. They called us to hand over all the weapons we had at the local commune in Drinjaca. People who had weapons went there and handed them in. They made a list on a piece of paper. They noted down the make of each rifle and its owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were there only members of the JNA or also members of a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but my brother was. He told me that everything had been in good order, that there was a major there who thanked them for handing in their weapons. He praised all the people who had brought in weapons, and he said that he would do his best to get them to go back to the companies and factories where they had worked before. He said, "You are loyal citizens. You won't have any problems." Some people were very happy to hear this. They were overjoyed because they would not be punished for having possessed illegal weapons and because they would be able to go back to work, because in those two months that had elapsed from the outset of the war, people had become very poor, they had become destitute. They hadn't prepared for war. I know my village well, and people weren't really that prosperous, that well off. They all had small salaries in the local factories, so they could barely make ends meet anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: After this date, you say that you slept for one month in the wood, so were there any changes in the village after this date, regarding the daily life, the work life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the town of Kula, the last strongholds of the Bosniaks defending the town fell on the 29th of April, everything suddenly changed as regards relations with the Serbs. They felt encouraged. People had to beg them for information, beg them to tell them whether there was any food to be bought, and they would say, "We don't know anything right now, but probably those who have dirtied their hands would have to be held responsible under the law." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some people did try to go to work, and they got as far as the barricade in Karakaj, where they were slapped and insulted, and they returned home. Fortunately, none of the people from my village got killed there, but there was mis-treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Now let's move to the date that you said before, the 30 May 1992. Can you describe what happened that day? Did anyone come to your village on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1992, we returned to our homes from the woods. I was sitting there with a relative of mine, and we were listening to a Serbian radio station, Radio Zvornik. Up until that time, it had been a joint radio station, but now they called it "Serbian Radio Zvornik." Suddenly we heard the following information: All citizens from the Drinjaca-Kostijerevo local commune are requested to stay at home and not to panic because the army will arrive. We didn't know why, but the army would be coming to the village to check something. They said, "Be patient, cooperate with them, don't be afraid." We were upset by this information because we wondered why the army would be coming. We had handed in our weapons. But soon this news spread through the village. People didn't really believe it. They said, "Well, we've done nothing wrong, so why should we flee now?" But about an hour or a little more later - I can't be sure exactly how long - we saw a truck hauling a gun entering the village, and we saw some soldiers moving across the fields. They were firing shots; not a lot, but they were firing, and someone was yelling at them, telling them to stop firing. We panicked. We stood in front of our houses. Some people fled to a nearby wood, and the soldiers quickly spread through the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who were these soldiers? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These soldiers were wearing olive-grey uniforms, the uniforms worn by the reserve force of the JNA. It was no different from the regular army. I had served in that army for a year, so I'm really familiar with that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you offer them any resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did they round up everyone, including the Serbs of your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We waited for them in front of our houses, and when they arrived at the front of the house, they would simply tell us to put our hands up, which we did. They would look to see what we had in our bags, because we always had bags ready so we could flee to the woods, if need be. But this time we were sort of resigned. We saw there was nowhere to flee to. They were rather rough with us. Let me just tell you a fact. A soldier kicked my brother in the stomach just because he couldn't reply to the greeting, "God be with you." And I tried to whisper the correct response to him, but he didn't know what to say. He was young and he'd never heard that, so he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us all to in front of a house, a house belonging to a Bosniak, and his name was (redacted), and they collected us up there, from wherever area we had come from. They gathered us together in front of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many people were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were about -- counting the women and children and men, about 150 of us in that part where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you see who commanded these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when those soldiers surrounded us, when they were standing around, I noticed a young man. He had a Motorola. He might have been 25 years old, something like that. Anyway, he had a Motorola and he was wearing camouflage equipment, and he would talk to someone over that Motorola fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Please, can you repeat exactly the name of the -- yes, Your Honour. My colleague was suggesting me to redact the name of the -- in the line 2, page 80, because it was possible to identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're absolutely right. Madam Registrar, could you please redact line -- page 49, line 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you hear this man talking on his Motorola?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't quite understand what they were saying. He was about ten metres away from me, so I didn't understand what they were talking about. But the last time they talked, I did hear him confirm something. He said something in the affirmative and said, "Drinjaca," and said there were a lot of them. He mentioned the word "Drinjaca."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he issued an order, telling us to get up, to stand up, and then he said that the men should pick up the children, take them up in their arms, and to form a column of men and women, and if they were husband and wife, they could stand next to each other, but that the man should carry the child. And then he said, "We're going to Drinjaca."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we please have the photo bearing 65 ter number 4150 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you recognise the building depicted on this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the cultural centre in Drinjaca, which is where we were incarcerated. We were put up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this photo into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P475.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did you arrive to this building, to the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was -- well, it's difficult to tell you the exact time, but I think that it was around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When you arrived at this Dom Kulture, were there other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went into the cinema hall, there was nobody there, but there were soldiers in uniforms from the reserve force of the JNA outside, and I recognised some Serb neighbours of mine, people from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you free to leave if you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you mean ? Explain what you mean. What place, to leave what place?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: To leave this Dom Kulture. Can you go out from this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we couldn't. No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did there come a time when other people were brought in the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cultural centre was packed jam full of people. They brought in civilians from another part of Kostijerevo, as well as Drinjaca, Sopotnik and Djevanje, so that the cultural centre was full of people, crowded full of men, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Approximately how many people altogether were gathered in the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say, but I think there were perhaps as many as 300, counting the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these people gathered in the cultural centre, and how did you learn it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Bosniaks, Muslims, and I know the people I lived with, all my own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Inside this cultural centre, without telling us the names or identifying them, or saying else that can identify you, can you tell us what other members of your family were present at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were my three brothers and my father, but I'd like to mention that one of my brothers was still a minor. He was only 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did there come a time when an army officer entered the cultural centre and addressed you people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer came by soon afterwards. I didn't know his name at the time, but he was wearing a uniform, the uniform of a JNA officer, and two stripes to denote rank. And he said: "You needn't be afraid. Nothing will happen to you. The situation is such that I have to tell you that you are going to be transferred to some villages near Zenica, and the Serbs who live there, they will come into your village -- your villages and your homes." Later on, I learnt -- well, two days later I happened to see the man on television, and his name was Branko Studen. He was a lieutenant by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened to the women and the children in the cultural centre? Were they allowed to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said at the time was this: "We're going to take the women and children outside now, and the men will remain. We'll conduct an interview with them, and then they'll be able to go outside too, and they'll be exchanged." And then panic followed. The women and children began to cry. They said they didn't want to leave their menfolk. He said, "Calm down, you needn't be afraid. They'll be done in half an hour and follow you out in half an hour's time." And so the women and children grew a bit calmer. We were separated from them. We said goodbye to them. They opened the double doors leading into the hall, and they all went outside. And when we men stayed on our own in that room in the hall, he said to us, "Don't worry. I know that you're not to blame for anything. I know how you lived here together with the Serbs. I heard all about that. You'll be exchanged, but before that some experts in military matters will come in to ask you some questions. So cooperate with them, answer their questions, help them in their work, and when they finish with you, you'll be able to go freely -- well, they'll put you onto buses and you're going to be exchanged together with your families."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened after Branko Studen had left the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After telling us that, he left the hall. A lot of soldiers remained, guarding us on both sides. They stood along the wall and they stood up on the platform and watched us from there. They were up on the stage, and they sort of played around with us. They would throw hand grenades about, pulling out the pin. Anyway, they asked for cigarettes. This went on for some time; not long.
