Suddenly, some people came into the hall wearing camouflage uniforms, whom I hadn't seen up until then. I noticed six of them, in particular. The leader, the man who was their leader, also wore a camouflage uniform, but he had a very big beard and sunglasses. And he rolled up his sleeves. He had a camouflage hat on his head. And judging by the uniforms, they resembled members of Arkan's units more than anything else, although I can't say with certainty that they were actually Arkan's men. But judging by their uniforms, and we were able to distinguish all these paramilitaries, I would say that was them. Anyway, when he entered, he went wild in the hall. He made a lot of noise, shouted. He said, "Come on, balija, on your feet, all of you." He started swearing. He used all kinds of swear words, and then he said, "Now I want to hear a song." And we looked at him, and he said that he wanted us to sing the song about General Draza Mihajlovic. And we knew that was a Chetnik song. I was a little taken aback. I didn't know what to do. I looked at the people around me, but the people began to sing this song. It's not a difficult song to sing. The rhymes are good. It's easy to rhyme. So can you imagine 91 people singing the song about General Draza Mihajlovic and his guards? And they laughed while they were singing, and then all hell broke loose. They would pull people out from where they were sitting. They would take people up onto the stage, onto the platform, and beat them. They beat people so badly -- well, as we say, they don't need a bullet, being beaten up that badly, they would die of the beating. And I just can't believe what the man was doing. He was either mad, or drunk, or drugged, but no normal person would behave that way. He was a beast, a beast of a man, and he was their leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Was only this man that beaten you -- that beat you, or also the other five, because there were six as you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all did the beating, but he was the only one walking around the hall, jumping up and down onto the stage, shouting, and he took Mujo Sabanovic, a neighbour of mine. The man was quite heavily built, he was over 100 kilograms, and he took him up onto the stage. And then all of them, in 15 seconds flat -- well, the man fell down, he fell to the ground and was unconscious. Then they would lift him up again, and then I saw something that astounded us all. I thought that would be the end of all of us when this happened. He took out a knife. I'll never forget that knife. We call it a Rambo knife. And he hit him three times with the knife in his right shoulder blade, and the man fell down to the ground straight away. Then they pulled him off the stage and pushed him to where he was sitting before that. And then they said, "Come on, bind his wounds." And the man sitting next to him - his name isn't important - he tore the T-shirt he had on him, and while he was bandaging up his right shoulder, I saw three holes from the knife and blood streaming down his shoulder. The man was trembling, and I thought he'd die any minute. That beating went on for a very long time, and it was already getting dark. I could see that when I looked out of the window. They did this at intervals, but in my opinion they beat up about 25 to 30 people on that occasion. They beat them up. And this man personally slapped everybody in the hall twice, showing them some photographs, people of -- people on photographs. I knew the people on the photographs and I could see that they were sitting somewhere, at some festivity, celebrating something, and there was an SDA party flag, that is, the Bosniak Nationalist Party -- well, not the Bosniak Nation Party but the party that secured the largest number of votes. And he said, "Tell us where they are so I can slit their throats like rabbits, slaughter them like rabbits." Nobody wanted to say who the people were or that they knew them. And then he said, "Right, you don't know who they are." And then he proceeded to slap everybody. He would take everybody in order, slap people one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were people beaten only by hands or also using other kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't use their hands for the beatings. I noticed various objects. They were quite close by. They had some sort of wooden batons. They had pieces of iron. One man had a police baton, a police truncheon. So beaten like that, you're done in ten seconds. You don't need longer than that to fall down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: During these beatings, did anything in particular happen to Valid Husenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm going to tell you now was really difficult to observe. I don't know how they happened to learn that he was present at the local commune, but, anyway, they beat him so badly, and it was all going on just two or three metres away from me, and so it was close by. I had the feeling that they weren't beating a human body, they beat him so badly, just as if they were beating -- they were hitting some plastic bags full of something. That's how they went at it. And then they said, "Look at them Ustashas." Well, we weren't Ustashas, but they said, "Ustashas, balijas, and they said look at your commander, look at what's happening to him." And then he said, "You, Commander, look at your army, look at your soldiers, what you've led them to." And he looked at us, all beaten, all black and blue, and then they continued to beat him. They beat him in several bouts, and at one point he said to them, "People, give me a rifle to kill myself with. I can't take this anymore."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: During these beatings, did anything in particular happen to Muriz Abidovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muriz Abidovic, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Muriz Abidovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was up on the stage. A soldier, wearing an olive-green uniform, I saw he had some cable 'round his hand. He took him to behind the stage, to a room there. That's where the dressing rooms were for people to get ready before their performance. And five minutes later, he brought him back. However, the man looked as if he was going to faint any moment, and so I concluded that he might have used an electric current to extract information from him. But, anyway, he was brought back in this terrible state. I don't know what he actually did to him, but as he had this electric cable or wire, then I assumed he did something with electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You said that in the hall there were also JNA soldiers. Did they try to prevent or to stop this kind of beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? At the time, we believed that the soldiers wearing the olive-green uniforms were, in a way, still part of the Yugoslav People's Army, judging by the uniforms and judging by everything else, the logistics of the whole thing, the command cadres. We knew that they were being mobilised to create some sort of future Serbian army, but we thought that it was still under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. Anyway, they did nothing. Their task was only to observe all this with their rifles. They didn't undertake anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How long did these Arkan's men remain for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said in my statement that they were Arkan's men, judging by their uniforms. It doesn't necessarily mean that they were. But judging by the description, the black gloves without -- with the fingers cut off, and the pistols they had, and the knives and the uniforms, they looked as if they were Arkan's men, but I can't say for sure whether they actually were members of Arkan's unit. But judging by what they looked like, they resembled Arkan's men. However, I can't understand why their leader, the one with the beard, why he would always insist upon "Chetniks," and us singing Chetnik songs, and he often mentioned the Chetniks. Judging by his appearance, he looked like a Chetnik himself, at least how we think of Chetniks, with beards and so on. However, I didn't see any insignia on his hat or anything like that, no cockade or anything, but the way he behaved was like a Chetnik. And on one occasion, while he was poking Muriz Sabanovic with a knife, he jumped down from the stage, and with this bloody knife that he had stabbed him with, threatened us and said, "You'll see what the Chetniks are this evening." And at that moment, I thought, well, can there be anything worse than what we've seen already. But when he said, "You'll see what the Chetniks can do," it could be analysed, whether he meant that he was a Chetnik or whether he meant that some other people -- some other men would come in who were Chetniks, I don't know. But they stayed in the hall until about 2100 hours, at least that's what I thought judging by the fact it was already getting dark. I could see outside the window, and it was raining outside and foggy, so it might have been around 9.00 p.m. Anyway, then they left the hall, never to return. But I'd just like to mention -- I'd like to tell you what the conditions were there. Nobody was able to go to the toilet. There was no water or food the whole day. And if anybody really needed to go to the toilet, then he would have to raise three fingers. I saw the symbol at the beginning of the war, I saw them make this sign with the three fingers, and I don't know what that means to the present day. And they had to say, "Sir," a Serbian soldier, "may I be permitted to go to the toilet." And if permission was given, the soldier would escort the person to the toilet and escort him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened after this man left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he left, they ordered us to keep our heads down between our knees and remain that way. And then they said, "If anybody happens to move, kill them straight away, shoot at them." And there was silence. About 15 soldiers remained inside the hall. Nobody else appeared for about -- well, for a long time after that. I'm not quite sure how long, but let's say 15 minutes, maybe half an hour. But this seemed to be an eternity, because my neck hurt me so much with my head down between my knees, so I can't really say how long it went on for. I could just hear the soldiers 'round about talking amongst themselves, but we didn't dare lift our head up. And then suddenly there was a noise of something hitting something or falling down, and somebody said out loud, "Lift your heads up," cursing our balija and Ustasha mothers in those seconds. We raised our heads, and in that moment I saw some men whom I hadn't seen up until then in the hall, and I felt that they were behind us as well and that they were coming in from the left side. And what I saw at that moment was people wearing olive-green uniforms, the SMB type, but different from the ones who were already there, they looked a little different. They had some wide trousers to above the knees, and some of them had some insignia, cockades. And I also saw on their shoulders some badges, and they looked similar to what they had on their heads. At the time, I wasn't -- well, it was just a matter of seconds, so you didn't dare look at them for too long. I was afraid to meet their eyes, that something might happen to me if I did, they could call me out or do something to me. So I'm telling you all this from my own viewpoint. Anyway, I was a bit anxious and I thought to myself, these must be Chetniks, so I kept that in my head bowed, and I linked that up to what the other one in the camouflage uniform with the beard said when he said, "You'll see who's going to turn up this evening, the Chetniks ." And suddenly he said -- or one of them said, "Heads down," and we put our heads down. And then they asked for ten volunteers to step forward. I was wondering whether to come forward myself, because I thought that they would ask the ten of us to bring in some food and water, because we had had nothing all day. I couldn't imagine that they had come to shoot us, to execute us. So I thought about this, and I said -- well, there's an old proverb. "Never be the first," it says, "and never be the last either, so always keep to the middle ground." And he said, "No volunteers?" And we kept silent. And he said, "Why don't you want to be volunteers? We have volunteers wherever they ask for us, we have volunteers anywhere and everywhere. We always want to be volunteers and you don't. Why don't you want to be a volunteer?" And we kept silent. And he went on and said, "If you don't want to volunteer, we're going to select ten of you," and then they started, "But you'll be sorry if you don't come forward and volunteer yourselves." And I heard that he counted out ten men, from 1 to 10, and felt them pulling these people out of their seats, and I heard them taking them away towards the exit. And then they started beating them there with their feet and with something else. I felt they were being hit with something else. And they said, "Quickly, outside." And then they swore at them. They cursed their mothers and everything else. They often referred to us -- well, swore at our Turkish mothers and so on. And I didn't know what was going to happen, but I heard that next to the wall -- you see, there was silence. When they were taking people out, there was silence. Just a few people were talking next to me. Anyway, they took us -- they took them outside, 'round the hall, and from the other side we heard a burst of gunfire. There was shooting. We heard that very well. We could hear it very well inside the hall. And then, I thought, that's the end of it. Five minutes later, they came back into the hall and asked for another ten volunteers. Nobody came forward. They said, "You don't want to volunteer? Right, we'll select you, then." And they took out a further ten men. They took them to the same place, more or less, and you could hear a burst of gunfire from automatic weapons, just as before. And then they came back again. They came back to the hall again. And this went on every five minutes. They would come back, take ten men out, take them to the same place, and kill them there. Well, I assumed that they killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who came to take you out, these Chetniks or also the JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: JNA soldiers, that is, the soldiers of the Serb army were there in that room, but also the others came, whom I recognised by their uniform. Let me say that I was in the fifth group, and I will describe you -- describe to you how I felt. I was beside myself, because I knew that the minutes of my life were numbered. Somebody hit me in the back with a rifle and said, "Get out quickly." I stood up. I didn't dare look at that man, and I hurried towards the exit. And I saw, in the room where there were no room -- no chairs, lots of water, because they had beaten people up there. Maybe they'd poured water over them. I don't know what they had done. They collected us all near the door, and then they ordered us to go out, to go outside very quickly. So we went outside very quickly. We left the dom. In front of us, there was a row of soldiers in olive-grey uniforms. I can't say that at that point in time I saw anyone with a cockade, but the ones who were taking us out said, "Go left," and the soldiers in front of us were holding rifles, and they weren't doing anything. When we got close to the place where we always heard the shots coming from, a man from our column, who was in front of us, said, "Men, let's flee," and right away we heard the command, "Shoot," and they fired shots, bursts of gunfire. And I was wounded in my right hip. I felt severe pain, I knew I had been hit, and I fell down immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened after you were hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What happened after you were hit in your hip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they had finished firing, I was down on my stomach, and I felt that they were still close by. But I was in severe pain. I was aware, however, that I hadn't been mortally wounded and I could hear what was going on around me. They were drawing closer, probably checking to see whether anyone was still alive. One of them kicked me in the back and said, "Oh, this one seems to be still alive." And someone who was a few metres away said, "Well, what are you waiting for? Fire a few more shots into him." And then a whole burst of fire was directed at my back, but they all missed except one bullet, which hit me in my right shoulder. The pain was so severe that I can't describe it. The shot was fired at very close range. And then something changed in my head and in my eyes, and I thought I was dying. But I could still hear their voices. And then I saw that, again, I wasn't dead. They started celebrating, they fired shots in the air, and then they went back into the room, and I assume they had gone to fetch the next group. I felt blood seeping underneath my body, and my reason became active. I thought they might pile up our bodies and burn them or bury us in a mass grave, so I tried to get up. However, this arm of mine was quite useless. I held it close, and I started fleeing. While I was fleeing between the school and a building where teachers lived, in the school playing ground, some ten metres away from the place where I had been hit, there was a large group of people. One of them was calling out for his mother, but I couldn't recognise his voice. It all happened in a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How were the condition of this large group of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all lying down on the concrete. They were all dead except for the one who was calling out for his mother. I don't know who he was. He was a Muslim who had been shot, executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: As you ran away from this building, from the cultural centre, did you notice anything in particular when you were still in the proximity, and what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was getting up on my feet, wounded as I was, and I was doing this really fast, in those two or three seconds I saw dead people around me. They were people who had been in my group, and probably as I had not been the first in the column, there might have been some from the previous group as well. When I managed to run away, wounded as I was, between the building where teachers lived and the school I had attended for eight years - I knew the terrain very well - I fled in the direction of my village over the fields. It was raining, it was nighttime. I moved along as fast as I could, although I was very tired and exhausted, but at one point I couldn't go on because of the pain and the exhaustion. I had to sit down. And then I looked at my wound and saw that it was huge. I put my finger inside and pulled it out again, but it was still warm. It wasn't so painful. So I put all my clothes on top of that wound and pressed it with my hand to stop the bleeding. And I heard at several intervals identical bursts of fire and the firing afterwards. I was sitting there resting, and suddenly I heard a man who was weeping, moaning, and saying, "People, what have you done? What is this, what is this?" He repeated that several times. And then they silenced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where did this voice come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The voice came from the place where the people had been executed. I think this must have been a Serb, because of course they wouldn't have allowed a Bosniak to yell at the top of his voice, saying, "What have you done, what is this?" But to this very day, I don't know who the person was, when he saw this horror of 90 people killed in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the bodies of those who had died, who had been executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume the following: Some 10 or 15 minutes later, a truck arrived from the direction of a shop in the vicinity of the cultural centre where the execution took place, and it stopped nearby. And I heard the sides of the truck being let down, and they were doing something there. It went on for about 20 minutes. They were doing something. I assumed they were collecting dead bodies. Later, the sides of the truck were put up again, and the truck went back towards the shop and then switched the engine off again, probably waiting for instructions. I assumed that they were collecting the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you describe exactly this second group that came into the hall before you were taken away; the uniform, if they wore some hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that some of them had those wide trousers, and even their collars were not like those on the JNA uniforms, the olive-grey ones. When I looked at the side, I saw cockades. I know what cockades look like. I had been in Belgrade. I had seen them being sold in stores. I'd even held one in my hand. I wanted to inspect it and see what it looked like. It's quite large and quite heavy. I saw that, but what Chetnik unit this was -- well, we knew they were Chetniks, but whether it was some sort of special unit, whether they were local Chetniks, or whether they were Chetniks from elsewhere, I didn't recognise any of the Serbs from my local area among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did they wear a particular hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I saw -- I saw caps which looked like the olive-grey caps, but they were a bit broader than that, and we recognised those caps as Chetnik caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when we say "Chetniks," I'm referring to all the Bosniak people. We see them with the kind of Chetnik uniforms I've already described, and cockades on their caps, because these were not worn by the regular units of the JNA or by the Territorial Defence units of the Serbian people which were later transformed into the Army of Republika Srpska. It was a paramilitary formation, that's how it was treated. For the most part, it consisted of volunteers. That's what they declared themselves to be. They always said that they were volunteers. But in my view, someone had to provide them with logistical support and someone had to recruit them, with the exception of certain individuals who wanted to put on such uniforms in spite of their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: To you, what's the difference between a Chetnik and a member of the Seselj unit or the so-called Seselj man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any difference. I can't -- well, in my view, there's no difference. A Chetnik is a Chetnik. They're all the same, as far as I'm concerned. I know that in World War II - we learned that in school - their commander was General Draza Mihajlovic, and there was a Chetnik army which collaborated with the German aggressors; but as for the Chetniks in this war, in our war, we knew who their chief was, the chief of that party and their chief, and I never distinguished between Chetniks and Seselj's men. In my view, they're all the same. I don't know who would be the commander of other Chetniks, if there were other Chetniks. I don't know if there were two kinds of Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Are you aware of anybody, other than you, that survived from what happened in the cultural centre that night? I will not ask you to mention their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, you have 12 minutes left, just for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll soon have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Before or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the best would be to break now. Then you can put things back into focus and think about it over the break in order to put the right questions for the end of your 12 minutes. Thank you, we'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Ferrara, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you make a list of all the people that you could recall were present that night in the dom, in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did make a list. I know a lot of people by first and last name, but I consulted some family members and then I made a final list of all the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Ms. Registrar, can we please have the document bearing 65 ter number 1382 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I wrote that. These are the people who were shot that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many people were shot that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening, 88 people were shot, and 5 others were killed while being brought in, in the course of the day, but I didn't include them in the list because I don't know how they were killed or by whom. That's why I made this list only of the people who were in the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Without saying the name, to avoid your identification, do you recognise the names of any of your relatives in this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here I can see the name of my father, three brothers, two uncles -- or, rather, two cousins, and there are others who are familiar to me:

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the document into evidence. I'll just point out to the Chamber the English translation of that exhibit does not repeat the names contained in the original. So in order to properly use the English version of the document, one must refer to the original. The documents must be under seal, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, a number, please, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P476, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we please have the document bearing the 65 ter number 2567 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you recognise in this document any name of any people who were present in the Drinjaca Dom Kulture on the night you have described until now? The second page and so on of that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I recognise them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You said that your father and brothers did not survive what occurred that night. Did you take part to the exhumation identification procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, in the identification procedure, but not the exhumation procedure. There's a special team that does that. However, in September 1998, all the family members were invited to Tuzla to assist the team for identification, so I attended that, and I immediately recognised my father and three brothers. And I want to say that half of them were in black plastic body-bags, so that even six years later the bodies were well preserved, and you could easily recognise the faces. I didn't know about such things before. I was surprised by this. It was easy to recognise them. The bodies that were not in bags were all squashed and unrecognisable, so DNA analysis had to be carried out to establish their identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the documents into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P477, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So what happened to you, left with gunshot wounds? Did you receive any treatment anywhere for these wounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received first aid from a man of Serb ethnicity on the second day, when I arrived at the Serb village some two kilometres away from my village. Everybody there knew me and I knew them, and there I found three school friends of mine in that village. That man gave me first aid. He dressed my wound. He gave me his son's shirt and pullover to wear, and I wish to thank him. I will never forget his kindness as long as I live. I wanted to thank him, because I'm quite well off. I want to help him. But he refused help. He said that, "All that matters is that you're alive." He really refuses to receive anything from me as a token of gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you receive any treatment in a hospital, and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was treated for a month and a -- well, for a month and a half they only dressed my wound, which refused to heal, and then on the 15th of July I crossed the occupied territory and got to the village of Nezuk, in Zvornik municipality from Cerska. And then I went to the clinic in Zvornik, and there I continued with treatment and physical therapy. They couldn't operate because it was very complicated, so that unfortunately I've been an invalid in my shoulder. I can't use my arm well, only a little bit, but there are jobs I can do with this degree of invalidity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we please have on the screen the document with the number 7244.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report from the orthopaedic surgeon. I carried it around in my pocket. It was folded four ways. But I can recognise my name and, yes, that's the document. It's the medical finding from the orthopaedic surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the document into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P478, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Just last couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What did you do after escaping from the dom cultural centre? Did you go to your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to my village, but I didn't go near the houses. At one point, I noticed some sort of soldiers with a lamp coming close to the houses, and very quickly they set fire to them. I don't know who they were, exactly, because I couldn't see what they looked like. I was about 100 metres away, so it was hard to observe who the people were, but I saw the houses set fire to. They moved in my direction, but they passed along the road some 50 metres away from me and went on to set fire to the other houses. I continued my journey. This went on until 5.00 or 5.30 in the morning, and I arrived at the house of (redacted), a school friend of mine. I saw there was no one there in front of the house, but I have to say before that I saw a Bosnian woman who had been left there by her husband and a neighbour. They ran into an ambush, and (redacted), was killed on that occasion, and she said to me, "Come and see this," and I said, "Well, I've seen enough," and that woman went off. Later I saw her on the free territory, and then I came to (redacted) (redacted) house, where I had a drink of water. I was very thirsty, and then I began to shake and tremble all over. And I took a nap in his barn, in his cow shed. When I woke up, the sun was out, it was warm, and I moved on. And I went to some neighbours of mine, and along the road I saw that all the houses had been burnt. I saw livestock grazing among the crops. It was chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we should redact the name of this woman in the line 14, page 103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Registrar, we need a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you ever reach the village of Mijatovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in that village. Nobody saw me. That's very odd. After that night, after what happened in that village of mine, two women recognised me, and they quickly gathered 'round me and offered me help. They mentioned my name. They asked what had happened. At that point, I did something nobody had ever done, and I'm still surprised at myself. I was probably already hallucinating. I had lost a lot of blood. I was exhausted, and I didn't care whether they would kill me or not, because at that point I thought that there were no Bosniak Muslims left alive anywhere. I thought I was the only one left, and I said to myself, "Why should I go on living?" But something else happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What else happened? Very quickly, because I don't think I have any more time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man who dressed my wound, he said to me, when I saw the others looking in a different direction, not looking at me, I should run away, because they had been ordered not to cooperate with any Bosniaks. But then I was approached by a Serb - I can give you his name, if you like - and he said, "You won't leave so easily because you're a witness to the execution and you'll talk." And I said to him, "Well, you have a rifle. Kill me, but remember, those are not 90 birds that somebody shot. People will be asking questions." And then another local person, who had been to school with me, swore and -- we had been good friends at school. He swore and he said, "Well, you see what happens. They come and they bring soldiers here, they do all sorts of things here, and then they go away and leave us here to fight with you." And I asked him what I should do next, whether he could help me, and he said, "Well, I don't know anything. They will decide over there." And then another neighbour, who still lives in my village, who's making up other stories, took me towards the neighbouring village, Paljevici, a Muslim village, and he said, "I'll see you off along your way, and then go on, I don't dare go any further," and I asked him, "What happened?" And he said, "Don't ask me anything. I don't know." Will we ever come back?" And he said, "Well, I don't know what laws the Serb authorities will pass about you Muslims," and we went to a field and he was already pointing his rifle at me and I saw he was about to kill me. And he fired a bullet right away, but fortunately he had an M-48 and you had to reload it each time, because all the others I saw had automatic and semi-automatic. He had to keep loading, but each time he missed me. And I suddenly felt strength to run away because my life was at risk. I crossed the river, I fled over streams and meadows. I saw him shooting on the other side of the river. He thought I was close by. He thought he would -- I would start running and he would see me and kill me. And the saddest thing is that man is still living there, and he's making up a story. He says he saw me off. He says he didn't try to kill me. Well, then, why did he run after me for 300 or 400 metres and keep shooting at me? Why didn't he say, "I've been ordered to kill you. I'll fire shots in the air and you can run away." He never did that, he never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, before we move on to the cross-examination, I just have one question for you to clarify; namely: What happened to the women and children who were taken out of the dom, cultural centre, before the beatings of the men began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those women were taken out, and as far as I heard from my wife later on, they were put into buses -- they crammed them into one bus, they could barely stand, there were so many of them, and they were driven away to Celopek, near Zvornik. That's a Serbian village, and they were held in some barns or sheds belonging to a factory farm. They stayed there for three days in these poor conditions with the children in these barns. They slept there. And then later on, they let them go to the free territory, which is the separation line, the villages of -- the separation line between the BH Army and the Bosnian Serbs, and they let them go there. But I have to add also something that surprised me. Our people surprised me. They saw some things from their own angle of vision, and they don't want to testify, and some women, too -- I had heard that some young girls had been raped there. However, nobody wants to testify and talk about that. And I can't do it because I wasn't there, I didn't see it happen. But there were rumours going around. However, the women don't wish to testify. For what reasons, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure it must have been terrible for them, but my question went to know whether they survived. And I understand from you that at least most of them, most of the women and children, did so. Did you catch up with your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well -- well, all of them were released. They're all alive and well. Now, what conditions they were kept in for the three days, that's another story again. However, after a month and a half, I met up with my wife. They didn't know that, they didn't know that I had survived, that I was still alive, because there was no way in which information could be passed on to free territory, where the BH Army was controlling the area. It was 40 kilometres up in the woods, and they didn't know that I was alive. So when I met up with my wife, when I went to Tuzla and they heard that I was alive, it was happiness and a shock and a feeling I will never forget, because I had a little baby, an eight-month-old baby at the time. It was terrible, but we were so happy that tears of happiness ran down our faces. The women cried, although many of their folk didn't survive. They asked me what happened to their relatives and people, and I said, "Don't worry, they'll come back alive. They've been captured." I thought up a story just to calm them down, because how could I tell them, "Your sons and husbands have all been executed"? There would have been panic all round and there would have been chaos. They would have fainted and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I need to consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one question to put to you, sir. You told us about this execution which occurred at several stages, and obviously you're a survivor. What could be surprising, when listening to your story, is the bestiality of this execution. It seems that everything was done extremely methodologically, in a very methodological way, and I wonder why. So in your area beforehand, were there any fights pitting Muslims against the Serbs, which may have justified such horrible retaliation? As far as you know, were there any of those fights beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For all the time I spent living there, the 22 years, I never heard that the Muslims, the Bosniaks, and Serbs fought for any reason at all. Well, just imagine how we lived. We lived together in such a way that when we were working out in the fields, if you were working with the Bosniaks, Muslims, the Serb women would cook us lunch, and vice versa. We'll help each other out. We would celebrate young men going to the army. Our Muslim women would dance with Serb young men at festivities and holidays and so on. We got on so well together that I really can't say anything here that wouldn't be the truth, that there were any conflicts or that it was terrible. There absolutely was none of that before. I really can't say there was, and I would tell you if there was something that might have caused this kind of situation or people taking revenge for some reason and so on. And in World War II -- well, my father told me how his father, that is to say, my grandfather, was killed by some four Chetniks whom his mother knew. They were from a nearby village, and they just called them to bring his documents, his wallet with his documents later on, so I really don't know. They helped each other. And I heard them -- people say that during World War II, some Ustashas would turn up and they would hide the Serb peasants. People helped each other. But in this war, it was quite a new version of events. Something quite different happened. There must have been some plan according to which these things took place. We fought for a big Yugoslavia, a joint country of all the nations and nationalities, whereas in this war everybody wanted to gain something for themselves without worrying about the means used to the end. Unfortunately, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this answer. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1064, I'm going to ask you one or two questions about the latest thing -- the last thing you just said. You said that your grandfather, during World War II, was killed by the Chetniks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you not perhaps make a mistake? Your grandfather was killed after the Second World War as an Ustasha, and he was killed by Ozna, O-Z-N-A, which was the communist -- or a form of communist police; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Your grandfather took part in the slaughtering of Serbs and taking Serbs from away from the village of Lijesanj, Kostevo [phoen], Mijatovo Brdo to be slaughtered, Djevanje, Drinjaca, Srpska Kamenica and other villages around Drinjaca. For example, he took part in the slaughter of 38 members of the Ostojic family from Drinjaca, 25 from the Mladjenovic family, the complete destruction of the Simic family; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I object to the question about the grandfather of the witness. I think this is really not relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It cannot be irrelevant because the Presiding Judge -- Mr. President, you started this topic, you broached the topic, you asked what the cause was. The causes of the hatred are very deep-rooted and are to be found in the Second World War. I am not justifying retaliation or revenge of this sort, but since you raised the question, let me tell you that I have a lot of information about that. And it's not the only place where this kind of terrible revenge took place. I'm not justifying the revenge but you broached the subject, so I had to follow on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's true, I did want to know the reasons for what had happened, and I did put this question to the witness. But the witness did not really answer very accurately. However, the accused believes that among these reasons, there's probably some elements rooted in World War II. I know absolutely nothing of this. I believe that maybe the witness does not know any of this either, or much of it. Witness, did you know any of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me just tell you this: I am so surprised with this question and all this information that I really don't know what this is all about, because let me tell you one thing. You know that after -- or, rather, during the former Yugoslavia, well, somebody would have told us in my family. We would have known about it. They would have said, "You did such-and-such." So we would have expected the Serbs to tell us that, "Your grandfather did such-and-such," whereas I'm astounded at hearing this piece of information. It's quite unbelievable. I have no words to express my feelings. This is terrible. Well, according to his information, 200 people were killed, and my grandfather was responsible. My grandfather worked in a mill, so how -- him being an Ustasha and him killing people, well, some of my Serb neighbours would have told me that. They would say, "Your grandfather did that, and he was in such-and-such a unit, and we're taking revenge on that." No. When they saw me, the people took pity on me and said, "What's all this that's happening? It's madness."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I think it's best to move to something else. Move on to something else. Given what happened to this witness, I don't think you need to add any -- to add to his ordeal, so please put another question to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had a few more questions on the topic, but since you insist, I'll give up on them. But I just want you to know that there's the other side of the coin as well, because these are very complex issues, complex problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1064, you told The Hague investigators -- you gave a statement on the 15th and 16th of January, 2001, for the first time; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the first statement. I think it was the second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The second was on the 22nd of May, 2003. I have both those statements.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think the first one was in 1996, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1996, you didn't give any statement to The Hague investigators.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember giving a statement in Tuzla in 1996, to a man who introduced himself as working for The Hague Tribunal, and I gave him a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then The Hague Tribunal did not disclose that statement that you gave to the Tribunal in 1996. They haven't disclosed it to me. Now, whether this statement exists or does not, I don't know that, I can't know that. I was given two statements that you gave to The Hague Tribunal. If the Tribunal has a third statement that you gave to The Hague Tribunal, dating back to 1996, they can tell us so straight away. But to the best of my knowledge, that statement does not exist. There was no 1996 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes. The statement is December of 1996, but it was not a statement given to the ICTY investigator, but to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was disclosed to the accused on the 20th of July, 2007, and it has received number 59. It exactly is the statement given to the Agency for Investigation, Documentation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sector 8, Tuzla. So it's not an ICTY investigator.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, so the Prosecutor has, in fact, confirmed my point. You just gave two statements to The Hague Tribunal. The first was on the 15th and 16th of January, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in that statement, you make no mention of Seselj's men at all; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Now, on page 6 of that statement, paragraph 3, you describe the arrival of this other unit which conducted the executions later on, and this is what you say: "When Arkan's men left, 15 minutes later another military unit arrived. There was about 30 men, and they were wearing Chetnik uniforms. On their right sleeve, they had the insignia of the White Eagles, and on their caps, large cockades. They were all between 20 and 30 years of age." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have to explain with respect to the White Eagles. Later on, I consulted people to see what they were wearing, and people told me well quite possibly they were these White Eagles, although I -- it's all the same to me. Whether they're Chetniks and Seselj's men, I make no distinction between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm clear on the fact that you don't distinguish between the White Eagles, the Chetniks and Seselj's men. All I'm doing is observing what you said on different occasions. Now, the fact that you don't distinguish between them, that's all right, too. Now, in the statement of the 22nd of May, 2003, that you gave to The Hague investigators, you make no mention of Seselj's men at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never called them "Seselj's men," "Seseljevci."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, in 2003, you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic trial; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have here the extensive transcript of your testimony provided by the Prosecutor, and there, too, not in any place do you mention Seselj's men; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, but I have to tell you one thing. Do you think somebody's going to say to me, in the hall, "Listen to us, we were sent by Seselj, and, here, let me show you our ID cards to prove that we were sent by Seselj." Nobody's going to say that, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to do guesswork. I'm just drawing your attention to certain facts that have been documented. So there are two statements given to The Hague Tribunal by you in which you make absolutely no mention of Seselj's men, and then there is testimony during the Slobodan Milosevic trial where you never, ever mention Seselj's men at all. Now, the day before yesterday, here in The Hague you talked to the representatives of the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they put it to you and suggested to you that you should say today that as far as you're concerned, all the Chetniks were Seselj's men, because you can't distinguish among the Chetniks themselves; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1060 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I object absolutely this kind of question. We didn't put anything in the mouth of the witness. We didn't suggest anything to the witness. We wrote a proofing note. We disclosed the proofing notes to the Trial Chamber, to the accused, where we clarify what does it mean for Chetniks, for Seselj men and so on. So I ask that this kind of a sentence in the statement of the accused will be immediately redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, my question cannot be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Let me go back to the meeting you had yesterday with the OTP in order to prepare this hearing. Mr. Ferrara just told us that you gave some details. Now, what is extremely important is the following: We need to know whether when the term "Seselj's men" appeared, whether you volunteered this of your own will or whether it is the Prosecutor who said, "In your statement when you're talking about Chetniks, you should please tell us exactly who they were," and then you would have answered, "Among Chetniks, there were Seselj's men." So we need to know exactly what happened yesterday. How was this topic addressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be quite frank, how this came about. The man did ask me that I should explain to him what "Seselj's men" meant, "Seseljevci," and what "Chetniks" meant, and I answered the following: As far as I'm concerned, me personally, I can't distinguish between "Seselj's men" and "The Chetniks." As far as I'm concerned, all Chetniks are one and the same. Now, whether he was recruited by Seselj or -- the ones I mentioned earlier on, or they put on the uniform because they wanted to, I can't know that. They didn't show us their ID cards saying, "We're Seselj's men, here you are," or, "I'm another sort of Chetnik," or whatever. That's not what happened. However, when people talk about that, when they know who their boss is, who the leader is, for example, you know today in Bosnia-Herzegovina there's the Serbian Radical Party and it's called "The Serbian Radical Party of Dr. Vojislav Seselj," and I saw this on television quite recently. Everybody wears T-shirts with Vojislav Seselj, and the parliamentarians all wear T-shirts with "Seselj" on them, so this exists in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I can tell you that I personally make no distinction between Seselj's men and Chetniks, because as far as I was concerned it was a surprising question when I heard it from the Prosecutor. I said to him, quite rightly, the man wanted me to explain. I can't explain. Now, whether the people were recruited by Seselj or who, I don't know. As far as I'm concerned, if someone's a Chetnik, he's a Chetnik and they're all the same. You have Chetniks, you have Arkan's men, you have this reserve force that was to be formed later on, the Army of Republika Srpska, Yugoslav People's Army. I know of no other military formations. So let's clarify this. As far as I'm concerned, and I can confirm this here and now, a Chetnik and a Seselj's man are not interesting. It's all the same to me. Now, the fact that someone were recruited by Seselj, for example, and then were called "Seseljevci" or "Seselj's men," I never heard them say, "Listen here, we're Seselj's men," I never heard anybody put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just to make sure we understand you correctly, you also mentioned during your testimony "Arkan's men." Are they also Chetniks, in your view, and is there any distinction or difference between "Arkan's men" and "Seselj's men"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do distinguish uniforms from Arkan's men, what I saw on the battlefront of Croatia and on television. It's easy to distinguish between them. I can't say Arkan's men were Chetniks. Now, in Drinjaca, in that cultural centre, I can't say that they were mobilised by Arkan, for example, because someone might put on a uniform just for the hell of it because they liked the uniform, without being in the unit. They liked to resemble Arkan's men, for example, or they like to look like Chetniks, because the Chetniks in Bosnia and Croatia -- well, somebody might like to look like that, but I don't want to guess. I don't know who mobilised them. But I do distinguish Arkan's men's uniforms, the Chetniks' uniform, and regular JNA units and the uniforms they wore, and the future Army of Republika Srpska. So I see four different formations, and I distinguish four different units. Now, whether people call themselves "Chetniks," or "Seselj's men," I heard people say, our Bosnian, Bosniaks, say, "Seseljevci," "Seselj's men," because they know that Seselj is the head of the Radical Party producing those Chetniks, sending them to the battle front. So they declare themselves as volunteers. Now, whether they're volunteers under Seselj, whether Seselj's suggested this to them, I don't want to enter into that. It's not up to me, and I can't know things like that. But things are quite clear. And let me state again, that's my view, that's how I view Chetniks, how I see them. Now, if there's someone else, another Chetnik vojvoda, for instance, who had special insignia and -- then I wouldn't say that they were Seselj's men. I would say that they belonged to this other man. But we know of no other man who was involved in this or meddled in Vojislav Seselj's business. Now that there are Chetniks in Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia and all over the place, we know of only one boss, one head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness. One last question before I hand the floor back to Mr. Seselj. When you were detained, yourself, your brother, your father -- or your brothers, your father, your cousins, and before you, yourself, were shot at, and you survived and fled, did you hear, from the people who arrested you, that they were Seselj's men? Had you ever heard anything like that, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard them say of themselves that they were Seselj's men or any other person's men. It lasted for a very brief moment. They entered and started calling people out. They didn't introduce themselves and say who they were or who their boss was. Why would they have to tell us that, when we're not going to need it anymore, anyway, because we knew -- well, when I saw them, I knew it was the end. And I'd heard all kinds of stories from World War II in my village about men like that, so I could guess what was going to happen. And I said during my testimony once -- I said to myself, "This is the end," because they have no mercy. When they appear, they leave nothing alive after them. They have absolutely no mercy. You can plead as much as you like. You're just a balija, as far as they're concerned, or a Turk, or whatever, and they have no mercy. I have -- whether they call me a Turk or not, I have nothing to do with that, but that's what they appeared to be, and I knew what was in store and what their aim was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness. Witness, tell us, when is it that you heard for the first time mention about the Seseljevci? Was it during the war, after the war, was it only now? When was it that you have heard this expression or term for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say with any certainty. Later on, I joined the defence of my country in the way in which I could contribute to my country. Let me put it this way: Quite frankly, "Seseljevci" wasn't a word mentioned often. Some Seseljevci were mentioned, but let me state again we Bosniaks only know of Chetniks, and we're not interested in any other names that they might be called. We just refer to them as Chetniks. Now, whether they're Seselj's men or whoever, how can we distinguish between them and say, "These are Seselj's men"? Nobody's going to come up to you and say, "We're Seselj's men," nobody's going to say that, but the uniforms were the kind they were, and uniforms speak words. I can't say that they were American marines if they were not. Looking at the uniforms, we know who was what. Now, whether their boss was Seselj or not, we couldn't know that, and they're not going to say, "Wait a moment, you're going to be attacked by Seselj's men." Heaven forbid, that's not what they would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: -- Mr. Seselj said that the first time the witness referred to Seselj's men was yesterday. The witness, in a statement given in 1996, called this man that entered the scene --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'd like to finish, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please -- he cannot finish his sentence. The Prosecutor cannot introduce by the back door material from the Muslim Security Service. He cannot be allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, wait just a moment for Mr. Ferrara. Mr. Seselj, you were calm so far. I would like you to stay that way. Now, Mr. Ferrara is telling us something, mentioning a document from 1996. I don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj said the first time the witness spoke of Seselj's men was yesterday during the proofing, or two days ago. In 1996, the witness gave a statement to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let the Prosecutor finish what he has to say, and then you will state your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Gave a statement on the 2 -- 2nd of November, 1996, to the agent of investigation and document of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Tuzla, and there he mentioned -- he indicated these men as Seselj's men two times, in the English version and also in the B/C/S version. They are called "Seseljevci." So it's not the Prosecutor that mentioned for the first time the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Mr. Seselj -- yes, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: The premise of the question is misleading the -- the witness, because he said that, "You never mentioned the Seselj men," before the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the floor. It seems that the document in which this was mentioned in 1996 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, you know very well that this behaviour by the Prosecutor is impermissible. He's referring to a document of the Muslim Secret Police. At the proofing session, he considered this document with the witness, and the witness corrected the content of that document, allegedly. That's what transpires from the proofing notes I was given, in the first paragraph. If it's correct that this witness gave that statement to the Muslim authorities, he said that all the Serb soldiers who were there were Chetniks, all of them. And now, allegedly, the witness is correcting himself and says, "When in the statement it says 'Chetnik,' referring to the people in front of the cultural club and during the counting, this does not refer to Seselj's men." The witness clarified he didn't use this term when he made the statement, but said "Serb soldiers" or "VRS soldiers." The person who took the statement must have misunderstood this. Some people used the term "Chetnik" to refer to all Serbs, but the witness does not do this. The witness even corrected the document of the Muslim authorities, which the Prosecutor does not have the right to use. The Prosecutor cannot use a document of the Muslim Secret Police. He has his own statements, two statements taken by his own investigators, and that's what he has to base his case on. And this is a double trick or attempted trick, but since I've unmasked it very efficiently, it's failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you met with representatives of the AID in 1996. Mr. Seselj tells us that that's the secret police, and the Prosecution states that it depended on the Ministry of Interior, they were able to investigate, but we will not go there. According to your memory, in 1996, that was almost 12 years ago, regarding the investigators of AID, would you have mentioned, yourself, the term "Seselj's men," or were they the ones who put that question to you or did they bring that term up? Because you were very clear earlier. You said that according to you, there were Chetniks, and there was the VRS, the JNA, but to your mind -- okay, you said that there were also Arkan's men, but you had not mentioned Seselj's men. But in 1996, did you mention that term or was it the police officer who put that in your statement? Do you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember I gave that statement a very long time ago. I think it was a matter of terminology. If I said "Chetniks," I don't know whether someone suggested this or if someone used the term "Seselj's men." I can't remember now. But if somebody wrote down that I said that they were Seselj's men, well, I say that I never distinguished between Chetniks and Seselj's men. It might be a matter of terminology, but let me repeat. I want to tell the truth. I'm not interested in anything else. I cannot say, if someone is wearing a Chetnik uniform, that he is Seselj's man, because he hasn't shown me a card saying he's Seselj's man. But we in Bosnia know -- for example, when we talk about Chetniks, we know that they have only one chief. It doesn't matter whether someone is said to be a Chetnik or Seselj's man, because I know they have only one chief and there are branches in Serbia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they all function as the Radical Party and they wear his T-shirts. If someone said "Seselj's men," I might have agreed, I might well have agreed. What I want to say is the following: I don't want to enter into the issue of whether someone is Seselj's man or not, because evidently I can't give the proper answer to that, but let me tell you that I consider them to be one and the same army, with a single chief at its head, and that's the most precise answer I can give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on my behalf and on behalf of my fellow Judges, I thank you for coming here to testify in The Hague. Thank you for telling us about these events that were so tragic for yourself and your family. Thank you very much, once again, and I wish you a safe trip back to your country of residence. I'm now going to ask the usher to escort you outside of this courtroom, and you may actually leave right now because the blinds are lowered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now going to ask Mr. Marcussen to tell us what is going on for the rest of the week. So we won't have any more witnesses for the rest of the week? Am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, there will be no witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we have a schedule that is in place for next week. We will inform the parties of our decisions regarding the witnesses that will come to testify as viva voce witnesses and who will come to testify under 92 ter. We have ten more minutes. Mr. Seselj, would you like to raise a housekeeping matter, if you have any? I don't know if you do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an issue, Mr. President. Whether ten minutes will suffice, I don't know. I thought I would have the opportunity of raising it tomorrow. The OTP has delivered to me a motion to have VS-1020 [as interpreted] -- that witness's statement introduced under Rule -- and I absolutely oppose this. I think that 92 ter cannot apply here, and I have not received the entire material. The last document here is not complete. This is addendum 5. It's a handwritten text dated the 8th of October, 1991. I have received only the first six pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Is it 1020 or 1026, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, 1112, 1112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, okay, 1112. Very well. There was a mistake in the transcript. So to confirm, it's 1112. Go ahead, please. So, in fact, no, the Witness 1112 is scheduled for the second week of July. We're not going to disclose his name, for the time being, but he is to testify over a period of three days. But for the time being, in fact, he is a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So, Mr. Seselj, upon consulting the legal officer of the Trial Chamber, there's a pending request, and the Trial Chamber has not decided yet on that matter. So I will not be able to tell you today what the outcome is for this motion, the motion being pending. The Trial Chamber has not ruled on it yet. But, in any event, it's quite simple. This witness will either come to testify as a viva voce witness or the motion under 92 ter will be granted, and that will be that. So for the time being, I can't tell you anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What would be useful, however, and this is what my fellow Judges are telling me, and I should have thought about it myself, actually, give us your arguments to tell us why you are against the fact that he testifies as a 92 ter witness, independently of your general position that we already know. But on that particular case, please tell us why you are against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Maybe this is a confidentiality issue. Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm sure the accused did not mean any harm but maybe if the accused needs to discuss the nature of the evidence of this witness, we should do it in private session and redact what has just been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
